title: Final Parking Space: 1978 Subaru DL 4WD Wagon

body_markdown:
Subaru of America[offers seven gasoline-powered models right now](https://www.subaru.com/index.html) , of which four are wagon-ish SUVs equipped with all-wheel drive and an outdoorsy image. Those four models (the[Crosstrek](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/2026-subaru-crosstrek-hybrid-limited-review-the-best-version-of-itself/) ,[Forester](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/2025-subaru-forester-sport-the-emotional-choice/) ,[Outback](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/first-drive-the-2026-subaru-outback-is-bigger-and-boxier-than-ever-before-but-is-it-better/) , and[Ascent](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/review-2022-subaru-ascent-onyx-edition/) )[accounted for better than 88%](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/subaru-of-america-reports-december-2025-and-year-end-sales-results-302652830.html) of American Subaru sales last year. The foundation for that success story here was laid a half-century ago, when the first four-wheel-drive Leone wagons hit our shores. I found a rare example of that car at[a Denver self-service yard](https://www.upullandpay.com/locations/colorado/denver/) last week.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


Because I live in High Plains Colorado, where corrosion isn’t severe and Subarus have been much beloved since the first 4WD models hit showrooms, I can[find examples](https://www.murileemartin.com/Junkyard/JunkyardGallery-Subaru.html) of just about every U.S.-market model the Pleiades-badged company has ever built in the local car graveyards. So far in this series, we’ve seen[a 1980 BRAT](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/final-parking-space/final-parking-space-1980-subaru-brat/) ,[a 1992 SVX](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/final-parking-space/final-parking-space-1992-subaru-svx-ls-l-awd/) ,[a 1987 GL-10 Turbo 4WD wagon](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/final-parking-space/final-parking-space-1987-subaru-gl-10-turbo-4wd-wagon/) , and[a 1981 DL hardtop coupe](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/final-parking-space/final-parking-space-1981-subaru-dl-hardtop/) .


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


Three of those FPS Subarus are Leones, but they are from the second and third generations of the breed. Today’s FPS honoree is a genuine first-generation Leone, a much rarer beast even in Colorado boneyards. I’ve spent years searching for one of these cars to shoot for this series, and now that time has arrived.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


Today’s article means that Subaru is now tied with Toyota and Volkswagen for the number of FPS episodes about imported marques. You can blame the influence of[my daily driver](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/adventures-in-unobtainium-jdm-repairs-plus-a-car-parts-briefcase-boombox/) for the fact that we’re looking at a Subaru instead of, say, a BMW today.


Fuji Heavy Industries


Subaru never used the home-market Leone name on their U.S.-market cars, even though every vehicle they sold here from the 1972 through 1989 model years (except for[the XT/XT6](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/this-trio-of-80s-japanese-sports-cars-could-have-made-their-mark/) and[Justy](https://murileemartin.substack.com/p/junkyard-jewel-1994-subaru-justy) ) was a member of the Leone family. With the exception of the BRAT pickup, Leones sold in the United States were called just “the Subaru,” and the trim-level designations were used as de facto model names. This confusing system results in even American fans of vintage Subarus using “GL” as the generic model name for all non-BRAT Leones.


When the bigger Legacy first hit our shores[as a 1990 model](https://www.autoblog.com/features/junkyard-gem-1990-subaru-legacy-wagon/) , the U.S.-market Leone finally got a model name of its own: Loyale. The Loyale continued to be sold[until 1994](https://www.thetruthaboutcars.com/cars/subaru/junkyard-find-1994-subaru-loyale-4wd-wagon-44497237) , after which Leone production ended forever.


大日本帝國海軍


Subaru traces its ancestry back to 1918, when the Nakajima Aircraft Company was founded in Tokyo. Nakajima and Mitsubishi built most of the aircraft used by Japan in World War II; the more diversified Mitsubishi survived intact after the war, while Nakajima’s assets were spun off into a number of separate companies. Those included Fuji Heavy Industries (which became Subaru) and the Prince Motor Company (which merged with Nissan in 1966). Subaru still[does plenty of aerospace work](https://www.subaru.co.jp/en/outline/about/aerospace/) today.


The Subaru story in the United States begins in 1968, when[Malcolm Bricklin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/we-talk-to-malcolm-bricklin-and-hear-the-hidden-stories-of-the-sv-1/) formed Subaru of America in order to begin selling[the Subaru 360 kei car](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/valuation/once-cheap-and-ugly-the-subaru-360-is-having-an-unexpected-moment/) here.


Subaru of America


The tiny 360 was a sales flop here, but then Subaru of America brought over[a bigger and more capable model](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QoTgejU2nIY) for the 1971 model year:[the FF-1 Star](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/subarus-all-wheel-drive-obsession-pipsqueak-ff-1/) . This car had a boxer-four engine driving the front wheels, a setup that proved relatively easy to convert to four-wheel drive[later on](https://japanesenostalgiccar.com/how-subaru-became-masters-of-awd/) .


The FF-1 was sold here just for the 1971 model year, but its successor crossed the Pacific a year later. This was the first-generation Leone, which shared the FF-1’s front-wheel drive and boxer-four engine (called “quadrizontal” by SoA for a while) but was significantly bigger and more powerful and thus better-suited for American roads.


The early Leone was still an itsy-bitsy car by U.S. standards, though, leading to this novelty song that got heavy airplay on[Dr. Demento’s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y-ByCrbFsYI) show in 1977, just when Weird Al Yankovic was getting his start there.


Subaru of America


Leone sales chugged along, increasing from 37,793 units in 1973 to 48,928 in 1976. Then everything sped up for Subaru of America, because 1976 was the first model year for the DL 4 Wheel Drive Wagon here.


Subaru of America


Oh, sure, post-1976 Subaru of America still pitched itself as a purveyor of sensible gas-sipping subcompacts, but the Leone 4WD wagon had no real competition and developed a cult following right away.


Subaru of America


By 1979, most American Subaru marketing was focused on this car (and its BRAT pickup sibling).


Subaru of America


Unlike the other four-wheel-drive machinery available in the United States at the time, this was a *car* , not a jouncy military-style truck deafening its occupants with a cacophony of oil-canning sheet metal and rattling toolboxes and punishing them with a kidney-killing ride even on pavement. Competitors shouldered their way into Subaru’s space during the 1980s, starting with AMC and Audi, but the image of Subaru’s outdoorsy go-anywhere wagon had become indelible, and the company was raking in fat stacks of dollars thanks to it. For the 1979 model year, total Subaru of America sales had shot up to 127,871 units.


Subaru of America


The second-generation Leone reached North America starting with the 1980 model year; the wheelbase stayed the same but the body grew a bit. A hatchback was added, the two-door sedan went away, and a dual-range feature was added to the 4WD cars. The second-generation Leone hatchback and sedan could be purchased with 4WD as well, although they never sold as well as the 4WD wagons.


Subaru of America


The second-gen Leone 4WD Wagon sold like mad in snowy regions of the United States throughout the 1980s, but there was one problem: drivers were expected to switch to *front* -wheel-drive when traveling on dry pavement, using a lever next to the gearshift. This was confusing to a lot of American drivers, who simply left the selector in the 4WD setting at all times and thus tore up their tires or worse.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


Subaru, along with many other manufacturers, developed a[true all-wheel-drive system](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/what-you-need-to-know-about-awd-vs-4wd/) that worked like Audi’s Quattro setup and began selling it during the late 1980s. Subaru called its AWD system “full-time four-wheel-drive” at first, and it was available as an option in the U.S.-market Leone beginning in 1987. Confusingly, the older non-idiot-proof 4WD system stayed in production in the Leone/Loyale all the way through the end in 1994; Subaru fudged this by using a character that could be read as a **4** *or* an **A** on its badging for that period.


Subaru of America


All U.S.-market Subarus were sold with all-wheel-drive beginning with the 1996 model year (this ended with the introduction of the rear-wheel-drive[Subaru BRZ](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/the-original-scion-fr-s-subaru-brz-is-the-millennial-generations-datsun-240z/) as a 2013 model), and so all the ingredients were in place for the hot-selling Outback of our current century: a reputation for reliability, wagons that evoked mountain trails more than suburbia, easy-to-use AWD, and boxer engines.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


Subaru began using the Outback name as an option package on the Legacy wagon for the 1995 model year. The following year, the top trim level of the Impreza wagon was named[the Outback Sport](https://www.autoblog.com/features/junkyard-gem-1998-subaru-impreza-outback-sport-wagon/) . The[Legacy Outback wagon](https://www.thetruthaboutcars.com/2021/08/junkyard-find-1999-subaru-legacy-outback-wagon/) proved increasingly popular, though its[Legacy SUS](https://www.thetruthaboutcars.com/cars/down-on-the-junkyard/junkyard-find-1999-subaru-legacy-sus-30th-anniversary-edition-45130033) ( **S** port **U** tility **S** edan) counterpart didn’t fare as well.


When the third-generation Legacy had its U.S.-market debut as a 2000 model, the Outback version was available in both[sedan](https://www.autoblog.com/features/junkyard-gem-2002-subaru-outback-h6-sedan/) and wagon form, and all external Legacy badging was removed from those cars (the[non-Outback Legacy wagon](https://www.autoblog.com/features/junkyard-gem-2002-subaru-legacy-wagon/) was still available). Sales of this generation of Legacy Outback wagon skyrocketed, and for 2005 the Outback sedan was gone and the Outback wagon became, simply, *the* Subaru Outback. Four generations and much SUV-izing later, the Outback is still with us.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


And so that brings us to today’s Final Parking Space car: the 2210-pound four-wheel-drive wagon that led directly to Subaru of America as we know it today (the[JDM Subaru lineup](https://www.subaru.jp/carlineup/?link=header-menu) is a somewhat different story, since it includes more non-SUVs plus a kei van).


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


I’ve photographed two other discarded examples of the first-generation Leone 4WD wagon, both ’78s and both in the same Denver yard as today’s car.[One](http://www.thetruthaboutcars.com/2013/11/junkyard-find-1978-subaru-leone-4wd-wagon/) showed up in 2011,[the other](https://www.autoweek.com/car-life/classic-cars/a38762969/1978-subaru-dl-4wd-wagon-is-junkyard-treasure/) in 2022. Many years have passed since I last saw one on the street.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


The weak point on these cars is their susceptibility to corrosion. In places like Maine and Michigan, they dissolved within a few years; in Colorado, where road salt is used sparingly and humidity is low, they held together longer.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


The engine is a 1.6-liter pushrod boxer-four, rated at 67 horsepower and 81 pound-feet.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


I would have taken more photos of the engine compartment, but the enraged wasps living in this nest on the hood hinge chased me away.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


The only transmission available in the 1978 DL 4WD Wagon was a four-speed manual. The front-wheel-drive Subarus that year were available with five-speed manual and three-speed automatic transmissions.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


This was the most expensive Subaru model sold in the U.S. for 1978, with an MSRP of $4968. That’s about $31,885 in 2026 dollars, which is more than the sticker on the current base Crosstrek and less than cost of the current base Outback. The cheapest 1978 Subaru was the base two-door sedan, which listed at $3368 (about $17,994 after inflation).


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


Subaru didn’t go to[six-digit odometers](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/ford-made-a-million-mile-odometer-just-for-new-york-state/) until a few years after this car was built, so we can’t know if this car drove 38,536 miles or 338,536 miles. The[best-traveled](https://www.murileemartin.com/Junkyard/JunkyardGallery-300kMileCars.html) Subaru I’ve found in a junkyard was[a 1998 Legacy Outback Wagon with 528K miles](https://www.autoweek.com/car-life/a65649323/1998-subaru-legacy-outback-wagon-junkyard-treasure/) , followed by[a 1999 Legacy RHD Rural Delivery Wagon with 431K miles](https://www.autoweek.com/car-life/a64733656/1999-subaru-legacy-rhd-wagon-with-431k-miles-is-junkyard-treasure/) .


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


Other than the extensive body rust and worn-out front seats, this car appears to have been in decent condition when it arrived here.


“Ooh, new Subaru! Got the brains and the beauty too!”


“I like it so much, I’d buy me two.”


Choice of skiers the world over.
